# Executive Summary
Current flood risk models generally assume that the shape of a flood is fixed, varying only in its maximum river flow. This project investigates whether this approach captures the uncertainty in flood events on the River Don at Parkhill, by considering both the maximum flow and the time a flood takes to reach its peak.

Using ten years of river discharge data, we identified 44 independent extreme flow events, across which both quantities varied considerably, with median values of around 106 m³/s and 44 hours respectively. Flood events were concentrated in autumn and winter, with autumn events typically taking longer to reach their peak, and we found only weak evidence of a relationship between maximum flow and time to peak, suggesting that larger floods do not necessarily develop more slowly.

These findings suggest that assuming a fixed hydrograph shape may overlook important uncertainty, so SEPA should consider incorporating variation in time to peak alongside maximum flow in future flood risk modelling guidance.

# Data and Exploratory Analysis

## Data Description and Quality

```{r tidying-the-data, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
tidy_data_table
```

The subsequent analysis uses 350,592 discharge readings ($m^3/s$) from the River Don at Parkhill velocity-area gauging station, recorded every 15-minutes between 1 October 2016 and 30 September 2026, covering 10 [water years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_year). Parkhill, the lowest gauging station on the Don, has a catchment area of 1,273 km$^2$ and applies a single peak flow rating curve to all measurements.

The dataset is complete, with each reading assigned a SEPA quality code (Table 1).

- Estimated ($n=14,915$): Retained. SEPA defines these as acceptable rating curve extrapolations where the river level exceeds the 3.7 m gauging limit, at which Good readings are capped (Figure 1), so they contain the largest flows and preserve the extremes.

- Unchecked ($n=162$): Excluded. These are restricted to recent entries (29 September 2026, 16:15 onward) and in sporadic 2017–2018 bursts of at most 45 minutes, and only two coincided with extreme flows, so removing them leaves a fully verified dataset with negligible impact.

```{r dischargeqc, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Discharge distribution for quality codes 50 & 100."}
qc_plot
```

From Figure 2 shows that discharge is low for most of the year, with a small number of large peaks, the largest reaching 418.68 $m^3/s$ on 19 November 2022. The distribution is strongly right-skewed (Figure 3), with a median of 14.73 $m^3/s$ against a 99th percentile of 130.97 $m^3/s$, suggesting that extreme flows behave very differently from typical flows and need to be analysed separately.

### Seasonality of High Flows

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", fig.width=6, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Median discharge by month (left) and total days spent above the 95th percentile in each month (right)."}

Median discharge is highest from December to February and lowest from July to September, while time spent above the 95th percentile is concentrated even more tightly to between October and February (Figure 4).

### Flood Event Hydrographs

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", fig.width=6, fig.height=5, fig.cap="The largest recorded flood event, showing the max flow and time to peak (left), and the largest peak in each water year, aligned at the peak and scaled by peak flow (right)."}
flood_anatomy_plot
peak_wateryear_plot
```

This introduces a key assumption that we will use throughout the report:

- Start of the rise: the last reading before the peak with flow at most $q_{\min} + 0.05\,(q_{\text{peak}} - q_{\min})$, where $q_{\min}$ is the lowest flow in the previous 7 days.

Figure 5 shows the maximum flow and time to peak for the largest observed event, and that the largest peak in each water year varies considerably in shape, so treating the hydrograph shape as fixed ignores an important source of uncertainty. Smaller peaks also cluster around each largest peak, so independent events must be separated.

# Threshold Selection and Independence

## Initial Threshold

The previous section confirmed the need to extract high flows, and to do so we use the Peaks Over Threshold (POT). This extracts flood events as the peaks of flow above a threshold $u$, and two common rules for choosing $u$ are the 95th percentile of flow and a threshold giving 3 to 5 peaks per year. Figure 6 shows both on the hydrograph, where the 95th percentile is `r round(quantile(q, 0.95), 1)` m³/s, and counting each period above the threshold as a peak gives at least 5, 4 and 3 peaks per year at `r crossing_threshold(5)`, `r crossing_threshold(4)` and `r crossing_threshold(3)` m³/s. At this stage, however, a single flood can cross the threshold several times, so these counts overstate the number of distinct events. Robson and Reed (1999) note that a threshold giving around five peaks a year leaves the flexibility to raise it later to exclude smaller floods, and the lecture notes that the threshold may need to change once independence has been applied. Since the 95th percentile gives `r round(length(candidate_peaks(as.numeric(quantile(q, 0.95)))) / n_years, 1)`, well above this range, we take the threshold giving 5 peaks per year $u$ = `r u_initial` $m^3/s$, as our initial threshold.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Hydrograph with the candidate thresholds. Peaks per year are counted before applying the independence rules."}
threshold_plot
```

## Independence of Peaks

To make sure each peak represents a separate flood, we apply the independence rules of Robson and Reed (1999). Two adjacent peaks are only treated as separate events if:

1.  they are at least three times the average time to rise apart, where the time to rise is the time between a trough and its peak, averaged over at least five clean peaks above the threshold; and
2.  the flow at the trough between them is at least two-thirds lower than the first peak, i.e. below a third of it.

If either rule fails, we treat the peaks as one event and keep the larger peak. In applying these rules, we use the following assumptions:

- Clean peak: a peak with no other candidate peak in the previous 7 days.
- Trough: the start of the rise defined in the exploratory analysis, which we use to calculate the time to rise.

At the initial threshold, the average time to rise is `r round(mean_rise_hours, 1)` hours, so peaks must be at least `r round(min_gap_hours, 1)` hours apart. This reduces the `r nrow(candidates_initial)` candidate peaks to `r nrow(peaks_initial)` independent events, or `r round(nrow(peaks_initial) / n_years, 1)` per year (Figure 7).

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Peaks above the initial threshold before (left) and after (right) applying the independence rules."}
grid.arrange(plot_before, plot_after, ncol = 2)
```

## Final Threshold

Since separating events lowers the number of peaks per year, we recheck the threshold using independent peaks only. Our initial threshold gives `r round(nrow(peaks_initial) / n_years, 1)` independent peaks per year, while Figure 8 shows that thresholds between `r min(thresholds_3to5)` and `r max(thresholds_3to5)` $m^3/s$ give 3 to 5.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Independent peaks per year at each threshold."}
rates_plot
```

To check which of these is suitable for extreme value modelling, we fit a Generalised Pareto Distribution (GPD) to the excesses of the independent peak flows $X$ above $u$, $$P(X - u \le y \mid X > u) = 1 - \left(1 + \frac{\xi y}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi}, \quad y > 0, \quad 1 + \frac{\xi y}{\sigma} > 0,$$ where $\sigma > 0$ is the scale and $\xi \neq 0$ the shape parameter, with $\xi = 0$ giving an exponential tail as a limiting case. If the GPD holds above $u$, the mean excess $E[X - u \mid X > u] = (\sigma_0 + \xi u)/(1 - \xi)$ is linear in $u$ (for $\xi < 1$), where $\sigma_0$ is the scale parameter at a threshold of 0, and the estimates of $\xi$ and the modified scale $\sigma - \xi u$ stay roughly constant as the threshold increases (Coles, 2001). [From Figure X, the mean residual life plot is approximately linear above ... $m^3/s$, and the parameter estimates are stable from ... $m^3/s$.]

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", fig.width=6, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Mean residual life plot (left) and parameter stability plots (right) for the independent peaks at the final threshold."}
mrl.plot(peaks$Discharge, umin = u_final,
         umax = sort(peaks$Discharge, decreasing = TRUE)[5])
gpd.fitrange(peaks$Discharge, umin = u_final, umax = 120, nint = 12)
```
Since the lecture notes that the threshold may need to change once independence has been applied, we lower it to a final threshold of $u = `r u_final`$ $\text{m}^3$/s, [which ...], giving `r nrow(peaks)` independent events (`r round(nrow(peaks) / n_years, 1)` per year), with fitted parameters $\hat\sigma = `r round(gpd_fit$mle[1], 2)`$ (standard error `r round(gpd_fit$se[1], 2)`) and $\hat\xi = `r round(gpd_fit$mle[2], 3)`$ (standard error `r round(gpd_fit$se[2], 3)`). [The diagnostic plots in Figure 9 show ...]
```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.cap="Diagnostic plots for the GPD fitted at the final threshold.", fig.height=6, fig.width=9, out.width="80%"}
gpd.diag(gpd_fit)
```

# Uncertainty Analysis (290 words)
The final threshold of $u = 65$ $m^3/s$ identifies 44 independent flood events over the ten water years, across which maximum flow and time to peak both varied considerably (Figures 11 and 12). Maximum flow had a median of `r round(max_flow_q[2], 2)` $m^3/s$ (interquartile range `r round(max_flow_q[1], 1)`–`r round(max_flow_q[3], 1)` $m^3/s$), while time to peak had a median of `r round(ttp_q[2], 2)` hours (interquartile range `r round(ttp_q[1], 1)`–`r round(ttp_q[3], 1)` hours) and ranged from `r round(ttp_range[1], 1)` to `r round(ttp_range[2], 1)` hours. This suggests that extreme flood hydrographs cannot be adequately characterised by a single peak magnitude or a fixed time to peak.

```{r distrubtion_analysis, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="The Distribution of the two parameters", fig.height=4, fig.width=12, fig.align='center'}
(Max_flow_plot + Time_to_peak_plot)
```

```{r uncertainty_analysis, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Max flow against time to peak, with a smoothed trend", out.width="85%", fig.align='center'}
Max_vs_time
```

Since both distributions are skewed and we are interested in any monotonic relationship, we used Spearman's rank correlation, obtaining $\rho = 0.287$ $(p = 0.059)$. This indicates a weak positive association, but with insufficient evidence of a monotonic relationship at the $5\%$ significance level, suggesting that larger floods do not necessarily take longer to reach their peak.

```{r cor_analysis, echo=FALSE}
cor_result_table
```

Autumn events (September–November, $n$ = `r sum(peaks$season == "Autumn")`) had a median maximum flow of 117.19 $m^3/s$ and time to peak of 59 hours, compared with 108.95 $m^3/s$ and 35.5 hours for winter events (December–February, $n$ = `r sum(peaks$season == "Winter")`), suggesting that autumn floods tend to take longer to peak (Table 3, Figure 13). With so few events per season, however, this difference should be treated with caution, and spring (6) and summer (1) had too few events to compare.

```{r season_table, echo=FALSE}
events_season_table
```
```{r season comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=12, fig.cap="A comparison of the uncertanity in the parameters by season"}
(max_season_plot + time_season_plot ) / Max_vs_time_season
```
```{r uncertanity table, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
results_table
```

Repeating the analysis at thresholds of 60-75 $m^3/s$, median time to peak remained between 43 and 47.25 hours and Spearman's correlation between 0.184 and 0.287 (Table 4), suggesting that the observed variability in time to peak is not simply a consequence of the chosen threshold.
